title: 3D Scanning Services for Plant, Tanks, Piping and Structures
description: Reality capture for plant, tanks, vessels, piping and structures: capture methods, the deliverable ladder from point cloud to digital twin, and how to scope it.
h1: What we scan, how it is captured, and what you get back
answer: Atlantis captures process plant, storage tanks, pressure vessels, piping, steel structures and whole sites using terrestrial laser scanning, drone and handheld photogrammetry, and mobile SLAM mapping. Output climbs a ladder: registered point cloud, mesh, as-built CAD, intelligent 3D model, then a maintained digital twin. Accuracy is set by registration control and the tolerance you specify, not by the scanner datasheet.
expansion: Scope a capture job from the decision it has to support and the rest of the specification writes itself. A clash check against a proposed tie-in tolerates centimetres; dimensional verification of a fabricated spool does not. The USIBD Level of Accuracy specification bands this explicitly, from LOA 10 at 50 mm through LOA 50 at 1 mm, and pairing an LOA band with a BIMForum Level of Development band separates how well the site was measured from how much of it was modelled. Those are two different costs and two different failure modes. A scanner rated at 2 mm at 10 m, the published figure for the FARO Focus Premium, still yields a wrong cloud when the target network is weak and registration error goes unreported. Ask for achieved registration residuals inside the deliverable, not the instrument datasheet, and name the exchange format: ASTM E2807 E57 travels between every platform.
source: USIBD Level of Accuracy (LOA) Specification v3.1 (2025) and Guide Document C120 for capture tolerance; BIMForum Level of Development Specification for modelling detail; ASTM E2807 (E57) for 3D imaging data exchange; API 653 Annex B for tank settlement survey layout and API 653 for shell plumbness limits; FARO published Focus Premium accuracy specifications; published research on bolted-target registration residuals.

facets.q: Which assets does Atlantis scan?
facets.a: Process units and pipe racks, aboveground storage tanks, pressure vessels, piping and spools, structural steel, jetties and civil works, plus whole-site walkthrough capture. Interiors, confined spaces and elevated structures are covered by drone and pole-mounted capture where standing a tripod in front of the surface is not possible. Marine, mining and fabrication-shop geometry uses the same pipeline.

facets.q: How is the capture method chosen?
facets.a: By what degrades first. Terrestrial laser scanning is selected where dimension drives the deliverable, photogrammetry where colour and surface condition carry the information, drone capture where access would otherwise mean scaffold or rope, and mobile SLAM where coverage of large walkable areas beats millimetres. Most industrial jobs blend at least two on the same control network.

facets.q: What accuracy should a scope of work state?
facets.a: Two numbers, not one. State a USIBD Level of Accuracy band for how well the site is measured and a BIMForum Level of Development band for how much of it gets modelled, applied per system rather than across the whole site. Then require the achieved registration residuals to be reported in the handover, which is the number that actually governs the result.

facets.q: What file formats are handed over?
facets.a: Registered clouds in ASTM E2807 E57, plus RCP or RCS for Autodesk workflows and LAS where survey software consumes it. Models arrive as Revit, IFC, DWG, MicroStation or plant formats such as PDMS and E3D. Every handover includes the control and registration report, the coordinate system, and the scan positions, so a later campaign can be tied to the same frame.

facets.q: How does a scan feed a digital twin?
facets.a: Geometry is split by system and tagged against the asset register, then inspection results are bound to locations on that model instead of living in unrelated PDFs. The binding step, not the capture, is the constraint: reconciling corrosion monitoring locations to real geometry is the work. Scanning a whole plant before that reconciliation is the standard way to overspend.

facets.q: What does a scan not tell you?
facets.a: Wall thickness, subsurface flaws, cracks, hardness, metallurgy and anything behind the surface. A scan measures where material is, never how much of it is left or whether it is sound. Geometry and condition are separate questions answered by separate work, and a capture deliverable that implies otherwise is being oversold to you.

sections.heading: The asset classes we capture, and what each is really asking for
paragraphs: Process units arrive as a geometry problem with a schedule attached — a tie-in that has to fit, a module that has to land, a scaffold plan priced before the shutdown starts. Storage tanks arrive as a code problem: shell verticality, roundness, bottom profile and settlement, evaluated against API 653 Annex B. Pressure vessels and piping arrive as dimensional control, where nozzle positions and spool lengths stopped matching the isometrics several unrecorded modifications ago. Steel structures, jetties and civil works arrive as a records problem, because the drawing set is lost, superseded or quietly wrong.

Each framing changes what gets captured and how densely. A tank settlement survey needs measured elevations on a defined layout — API 653 Annex B sets the minimum number of survey points at N = D/10, rounded up to an even whole number, with spacing no greater than 31.42 feet. A tie-in scan needs one small volume captured tightly and everything around it captured loosely. Scanning both at the same density is how a capture budget gets consumed by data that no decision ever touches.

We also capture whole sites where the deliverable is navigability rather than measurement: a walkthrough that lets an engineer three time zones away stand inside the unit, click a valve and read its tag. That is a legitimate deliverable with a legitimate and much looser accuracy requirement. Naming which of these four framings applies is the first question in any scoping call, because it sets the instrument, the station count, the registration effort and the deliverable format before anything else is decided.

sections.heading: Four capture methods, and the condition that selects each
paragraphs: Terrestrial laser scanning is the default for process plant, tanks, vessels and confined interiors. It produces ranged measurements rather than inferred ones, and it works in the poor, mixed lighting industrial interiors actually have. FARO publishes 2 mm at 10 m and 3.5 mm at 25 m for the Focus Premium, with a ±1 mm ranging error. Those are instrument figures, not project figures. What reaches your deliverable is that number degraded by however well the individual scan positions were tied together, which is a field discipline rather than a purchase decision.

Photogrammetry, handheld or drone-borne, wins where colour and surface texture carry the information: coating breakdown, corrosion mapping, weld cap profile, forensic and heritage documentation. Drone capture opens flare stacks, tank roofs, jetty undersides, cooling towers and bridge soffits without scaffold or rope access, and the access saving routinely exceeds the cost of the capture itself. The trade is that photogrammetric geometry is reconstructed from imagery and inherits every weakness in the imagery — texture-poor surfaces, specular steel and uniform coatings all degrade it.

Mobile and handheld SLAM mapping trades accuracy for speed across large, cluttered, walkable areas: warehouses, cable basements, mine workings, long pipe racks. It is right where coverage beats millimetres and wrong where a fabricated part depends on the result. Most real industrial jobs blend two methods on a single control network — terrestrial scanning for the units that drive dimensions, drone or SLAM for everything that only needs to exist. [Laser scanning versus photogrammetry for industrial work](/3d-scanning/laser-scanning-vs-photogrammetry-industrial) sets out where each one degrades first.

The fourth method is to use what already exists. Where the isometrics, the BIM model or a prior campaign are trustworthy and the decision at hand sits comfortably inside their tolerance, there is nothing to buy. Verifying the existing record against a handful of checked dimensions costs a fraction of a capture campaign and closes a surprising number of enquiries before they become projects. When that is the answer, we say so.

sections.heading: The deliverable ladder, and picking the rung you will actually use
paragraphs: Reality capture is sold as a single purchase and consumed as a ladder. Each rung is built from the one below it, each costs more than the one below it, and each answers a different question. The rung you buy should be the highest one a real decision needs, and no higher. Buying the top rung across an entire site is the most reliable way to spend a capture budget on geometry nobody ever opens, and the overspend is invisible until the model has sat unused for a year.

The move that matters is applying a modelling level per system rather than across the site. A tie-in area justifies object-level modelling with fittings, bolt circles and support steel resolved; the adjacent pipe rack rarely does. Requesting the same level everywhere multiplies modelling hours without changing a single decision, because modelling — not scanning — is where the hours sit once the crew has left site and the invoice starts growing.

The conversion from cloud to a usable engineering deliverable is a separate craft with its own failure modes: over-modelled geometry, objects that look correct but carry no dimensional fidelity, and models delivered with no statement of the tolerance they were drawn to. [Point cloud to CAD and as-built deliverables](/3d-scanning/point-cloud-to-cad-as-built-deliverables) covers how that conversion is specified, checked and accepted, including the acceptance tests worth writing into a purchase order.

sections.heading: Accuracy is a specification you write, not a property you buy
paragraphs: Accuracy in reality capture is not a property of the scanner. It is a specification you write and a provider proves. The USIBD Level of Accuracy specification exists precisely to make it writable: LOA 10 at 50 mm, LOA 30 at 15 mm, LOA 40 at 5 mm and LOA 50 at 1 mm, with the bands drawn from the tolerance ranges in DIN 18710. Version 3.1, published in 2025, added guidance on expressing tolerance as a standard deviation rather than a single figure.

USIBD also separates measured accuracy — how well the site was captured — from represented accuracy, how well the model or drawing derived from it reflects that capture. The two degrade independently. A cloud captured to LOA 40 and modelled carelessly delivers an LOA 20 answer, and nothing in the deliverable warns you. Specify both bands, and require the represented accuracy to be stated on the drawing sheet or carried in the model metadata where a later user will find it.

The number that actually governs the result is registration residual: how tightly individual scan positions were tied to each other and to site control. Published work on bolted-target registration reports mean residuals around 2.3 mm across a target network. Ask any provider what residual they achieved on your job, not what the instrument is rated for. [Scan accuracy and tolerance on an industrial plant](/3d-scanning/scan-accuracy-tolerance-industrial-plant) works through how the two relate and where error enters the chain.

sections.heading: Tanks and vessels: the geometry the codes actually name
paragraphs: Tank and vessel work is where scanning stops being a convenience and becomes the evidence base for a code decision. API 653 Annex B evaluates settlement from measured elevations around the shell-to-bottom weld, with the minimum number of survey points set at N = D/10 rounded up to an even whole number and spacing capped at 31.42 feet. A scan produces those elevations, plus every point between them, from one occupation rather than a manual traverse around a tank in service.

The same capture yields shell verticality, out-of-roundness, bottom profile and local distortion from a single dataset. API 653 places the out-of-plumbness limit for a reconstructed tank at 1/100 of total shell height, capped at 5 inches; an existing tank exceeding it requires an evaluation of suitability for continued service rather than an automatic repair. A scan gives that evaluation a dense measured input instead of a handful of spot checks taken where access happened to be easy.

The decisive advantage is campaign-to-campaign comparability. Two scans tied to the same control network produce a deviation map, which is evidence; two manual surveys with different reference points produce two opinions. That comparability is only real when the control network is re-established, so specify permanent monuments at the first campaign. Where the result then needs an engineering disposition rather than a repair, that work sits with [NDT and integrity consulting](/consulting).

sections.heading: Writing a scope of work a scanner can price and an auditor can check
paragraphs: A scope of work that a scanning contractor can price accurately and an auditor can check later contains seven things, and most published scopes contain two. State the purpose — the specific decision the capture supports. State the accuracy band, referenced to USIBD LOA. State the modelling level, referenced to BIMForum LOD, per system rather than site-wide. State the coverage boundary in plain language, including what is deliberately excluded and why.

Then state the four things that get argued about after handover. Require the control and registration report, including achieved residuals and the coordinate system. Name the deliverable formats explicitly — ASTM E2807 E57 for the exchange cloud, plus whichever native format your engineering team actually consumes. Set the handover medium and the retention period, because clouds are large and providers archive them on their own schedule. Finally, agree revisit terms before mobilisation, not after somebody finds a missed area.

Two clauses are worth adding on any brownfield site. First, require the scan positions to be recorded and delivered, so a later campaign can reoccupy them and produce a comparable result. Second, require a stated tolerance on any drawing produced from the cloud, printed on the sheet itself. Drawings without a tolerance statement become authoritative by accident, and three years later somebody fabricates against a line nobody ever claimed was accurate.

sections.heading: Where capture stops and inspection starts
paragraphs: A scan records surfaces. It measures where material is, never how much of it remains or whether it is sound. Wall thickness, subsurface flaws, cracks, laminations, hardness and metallurgy are all invisible to reality capture, and no increase in point density changes that. Geometry and condition are separate questions, answered by separate work, delivered on separate schedules — and confusing the two is the single most common misunderstanding on a first scanning enquiry.

The two are complementary rather than alternative. The capture tells you where a corrosion monitoring location physically sits and what geometry surrounds it; the examination tells you what the wall thickness is at that point. Both are needed for an integrity decision, and the record that survives an audit is the one where each result is traceable to a place and a procedure. Where the existing inspection records are the weak link rather than the geometry, [NDT report validation](/report-validation) is the faster fix.

sections.heading: From geometry to a twin that stays true
paragraphs: Geometry is the cheap half of a digital twin. The expensive half is binding condition data to it: reconciling the corrosion monitoring location register, the equipment tag list and the inspection history to real coordinates on a real model. Programmes that capture first and reconcile later capture at the wrong resolution, because the resolution requirement comes from how precisely a CML has to be located, not from how detailed the model looks in a demo.

Do it in the other order. Establish which units carry condition data worth binding and at what location resolution, then scan those units to that requirement and capture everything else at walkthrough fidelity. The result is a twin a reliability engineer opens weekly rather than a showpiece opened once at handover. [What a digital twin actually does](/digital-twins) covers the platform side and the data model behind it.

A twin also ages. Every turnaround changes geometry, and a twin that is never re-captured drifts silently away from the plant until somebody trusts it once too often. Build the re-capture interval into the programme at the start, scoped to the units that actually change. If you are still deciding whether a twin or an inspection data management system is the right container for the data, [digital twin versus IDMS](/digital-twin-vs-idms) sets out the difference.

sections.heading: Sectors served, and what each asks for first
paragraphs: Refining and petrochemical sites ask for tie-in geometry, turnaround access planning and tank programmes first. Terminals and tank farms ask for settlement, verticality and volumetric calibration. Power generation asks for turbine hall access, boiler and duct geometry, and outage planning. Marine and shipyard work asks for hull form, block fit-up and retrofit clearance in spaces where no drawing survived the last conversion, which is most of them.

Aerospace and defence work asks for tooling, fixture and jig verification against nominal, at tolerances an order tighter than plant work — which changes the instrument rather than the workflow. Fabrication shops and modular yards ask for pre-shipment dimensional control, because a module that does not fit on arrival costs more than every scan on the project combined. Mining and bulk handling asks for stockpile volumes, conveyor alignment and structural deformation over time.

What differs between sectors is the tolerance and the reason, not the pipeline: capture, register, report residuals, model to a stated level, hand over in an open format. Tell us the decision waiting on the geometry and the date it is waiting for, and the specification writes itself. [Talk to us about a capture scope](/contact) — demo and quote on request, and affordable, accessible and fully customizable across every asset class above.

faq.q: Can you scan a unit that is running?
faq.a: Yes. Terrestrial laser scanning and photogrammetry are non-contact and line-of-sight, so capture proceeds around live plant under normal permit conditions. What changes is coverage: insulation, lagging, congestion and no-go zones create occlusions, and the scan records the outside of the insulation rather than the pipe beneath it. Say up front which surfaces must be captured bare, because that drives scaffolding and stripping scope rather than scanning scope.

faq.q: What determines how long capture takes on site?
faq.a: Station count, not floor area. Congested process units need many short-range positions to see around obstructions; open tank farms and structural steel need far fewer. Access control, permits, escorting and working-at-height arrangements frequently exceed actual scanning time. A realistic mobilisation plan is built from a walkdown or a marked-up plot plan, which is the first thing we ask for.

faq.q: Do we need to provide site survey control?
faq.a: Not always, but the deliverable is stronger when you do. Tying capture to an existing plant grid or to permanent monuments means a later campaign can be compared to this one directly, which is what turns two scans into a deformation record. Without control, the cloud is internally consistent but floats in its own coordinate system, and every future comparison begins with a registration argument nobody wins.

faq.q: Can you work from a point cloud someone else captured?
faq.a: Yes, where the registration report and coordinate system come with it. Modelling, drawing production, deviation analysis and twin preparation all run on a third-party cloud in ASTM E2807 E57, RCP or LAS. Without the achieved registration residuals the cloud can be used for visualisation and coordination, but it cannot be defended as a dimensional record if a fabrication decision is challenged later.

faq.q: What happens when the scan shows the drawings are wrong?
faq.a: That is the normal outcome on a brownfield site and a large part of the reason for scanning. The deliverable becomes the corrected as-built record, and the discrepancy list is handed over separately so engineering can decide what to update and what to leave. Catching it before fabrication converts a site rework into a shop dimension, which is where the return on a capture campaign usually sits.

title: NDT Consulting: Level III Cover, Written Practice and Audits
description: The full ASNT Level III consulting catalogue: written practice, procedures, examination oversight, retained and interim cover, audits, programme build, succession.
h1: The engagement catalogue, the regimes behind it, and how work starts
answer: Atlantis consulting covers written practice authoring, NDT procedure development and demonstration, examination writing and grading, retained or interim Level III cover, programme audits and gap assessment, programme build for new inspection firms, and Level III succession. Work runs across SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, NAS 410, EN 4179 and ISO 9712. Method scope decides who can sign what.
expansion: Every engagement resolves to a document somebody has to defend. The written practice is the root: SNT-TC-1A requires the employer to prepare one and have it approved by the employer's Level III, and every certificate the company issues traces back to it. Procedures sit under that, approved by a Level III and, where the referencing code demands it, demonstrated before an inspector under ASME Section V Article 1 T-150. Examination records sit under those. The regime is chosen by the customer contract, not by preference: aerospace and Nadcap work invokes NAS 410 or EN 4179, contracts naming ANSI/ASNT CP-189 impose a standard written in shall rather than a recommended practice written in should, and ISO 9712 replaces the employer scheme with third-party certification held by the individual. Scope from the artefact backwards and the regime becomes an input, not an argument.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition) and ANSI/ASNT CP-189 for employer-based certification; ISO 9712 for third-party certification; NAS 410 and EN 4179 for aerospace and Nadcap-accredited suppliers; ASME BPVC Section V Article 1 T-150 for written and revised NDE procedures; ASNT published Level III recertification cycle and the 2026 update replacing the 2020 reference editions with 2024.

facets.q: What engagements does the consulting practice cover?
facets.a: Written practice authoring and revision, procedure development and demonstration, examination question banks and grading, retained Level III cover, interim cover after a resignation, programme audit and gap assessment, full programme build for a firm starting from zero, and planned succession before a named Level III leaves. Report validation and independent second opinions on disputed calls sit alongside these.

facets.q: Which certification regimes does Atlantis work across?
facets.a: ASNT SNT-TC-1A and ANSI/ASNT CP-189 for employer-based US industrial work, NAS 410 and EN 4179 for aerospace and Nadcap-accredited suppliers, and ISO 9712 where a customer requires third-party certification held by the individual. The customer contract selects the regime. Programmes that quietly mix two are the most common finding in a first audit.

facets.q: Who decides which regime applies to us?
facets.a: Your customer, through the contract and the purchase order. Aerospace primes and Nadcap accreditation invoke NAS 410 or EN 4179. Contracts naming CP-189 impose mandatory requirements rather than recommendations. Absent an explicit clause, SNT-TC-1A employer-based certification is the default across US industrial work. Declare the choice in the written practice and apply it consistently.

facets.q: What is the method scope constraint?
facets.a: A Level III is certified method by method, so authority is bounded by method. A Level III certified in UT and MT approves UT and MT procedures and grades UT and MT examinations, and cannot extend that signature to RT or ET. Programmes covering six methods need those six methods covered by certification, whether by one person or several.

facets.q: Can a consultant certify our technicians?
facets.a: No. Under SNT-TC-1A certification is an act of the employer and does not transfer to an agency, even when the agency writes the practice, sets the exams, grades the papers and approves every procedure. The consultant produces and signs the technical work. Your company signs the certificate, holds the training and experience records, and answers to the auditor.

facets.q: How does an engagement actually start?
facets.a: With a scoping call that names the artefact you need at the end and the date somebody is waiting for it. From there the regime, the methods in scope, the delivery model and the record set you already hold are established, and a written scope follows. Demo and quote on request; no engagement begins before the deliverable is written down.

sections.heading: The engagement catalogue, in full
paragraphs: Consulting enquiries land as one of eight jobs, and naming which one you have shortens everything that follows. Written practice authoring. Procedure development and demonstration. Examination oversight. Retained Level III cover. Interim cover after a departure. Programme audit and gap assessment. Programme build from zero. Succession before a named Level III leaves. Each ends in a specific artefact somebody has to defend in front of an auditor or a client, and each is scoped backwards from that artefact rather than forwards from a task list.

Two more sit alongside the eight and are frequently the real requirement behind an enquiry. [NDT report validation](/report-validation) is an independent technical review of inspection reports before they are issued, or after a client has challenged them — faster than a programme engagement and often the thing that was actually broken. Independent second opinions on disputed calls belong in the same category: one technical question, answered in writing, with the reasoning attached so it survives being forwarded.

The catalogue also has an edge, and it is worth stating. Where the honest answer is that no consultant is needed — the programme is sound, the finding is routine, the existing records already support the decision — that is the answer given. An engagement producing a document nobody uses is worse than no engagement at all, because it becomes a document an auditor will read and hold you to.

sections.heading: Written practice: the document everything else hangs from
paragraphs: The written practice is the root document. SNT-TC-1A requires the employer to prepare a written practice for qualifying and certifying its own NDT personnel, and requires that document to be on file and approved by the employer's Level III. Every certificate the company issues, every qualification decision and every examination score traces back to it. It is also, without exception, the first document a client or accreditation auditor asks to see when they walk in.

A defensible written practice states the methods and levels covered, training hours and documented experience by level and method, examination structure and passing criteria, near-vision and colour-contrast requirements, the recertification cycle, and records retention. Where it goes wrong is rarely omission — it is drift. A practice written against one edition, examinations run against another, and technicians qualified under rules the current document no longer contains. Candidates sitting Basic examinations after 1 January 2026 work to the 2024 editions of SNT-TC-1A and CP-189, which replaced the 2020 editions in ASNT's reference list.

Authoring is one document cycle; keeping it current is an annual review triggered by scheme changes, new methods, new contracts and new regions. [Written practice development](/consulting/written-practice-development) covers what goes into the document and how an employer formally adopts it. The regime it is written against, and what SNT-TC-1A does and does not require, is set out at the [SNT-TC-1A compliance hub](/compliance/asnt-snt-tc-1a).

sections.heading: Procedure development and the demonstration that qualifies it
paragraphs: Procedures sit directly under the written practice, and a Level III approves them. ASME Section V Article 1 T-150 requires written procedures for the examinations it governs, and requires a revised procedure to be prepared and approved by a Level III whenever an essential variable changes. That clause is the reason procedure control fails quietly rather than loudly: a technique is adjusted in the field, an essential variable moves, and the procedure on file no longer describes what was actually done on the job.

Where the referencing code section requires it, a procedure is also demonstrated — run on representative geometry, controlled by a Level III, witnessed by the inspector, and documented. Most ASME sections require demonstration to the Authorized Inspector rather than formal qualification, and the distinction matters because the two generate different records. Procedures are written narrowly enough to be demonstrable and broadly enough to cover the work you actually sell, which is a drafting skill rather than a code lookup.

Multi-method programmes need this repeated per method and per technique. UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT including digital and computed radiography, MT, PT, VT and ET each carry their own essential variables and their own demonstration expectations. A procedure set assembled from mixed sources — some inherited from a previous employer, some copied from a client, some written in-house years ago — is the most common finding in a first client audit and the slowest to close.

sections.heading: Examination oversight: writing, administering, grading, retaining
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A assigns the Level III responsibility for approving and grading the examinations administered for certification. In practice that means three artefacts: a question bank matched to the method and level being claimed, an answer key, and graded papers retained with scores, dates and invigilation records. Practical examinations add a specimen set with known indications and a recorded result against them, which is the part most often missing when a programme is inspected.

The examination record is where programmes fail an audit most often, and rarely because the examination itself was wrong. It fails because the papers were not retained, because the specific examination did not match the method or level claimed, or because the grading carries no signature behind it. An auditor is not assessing whether your technician can perform UT. They are assessing whether you can prove how you concluded that they could.

Examination oversight is scheduled against your qualification calendar rather than run continuously, which is exactly why it suits an outside arrangement. New hires, recertification cycles and new method additions cluster together; between clusters the workload does not justify a permanent appointment. Under SNT-TC-1A the recommended maximum recertification interval is five years across Levels I, II and III, which makes the calendar predictable enough to plan cover around.

sections.heading: Level III cover: retained, project and interim
paragraphs: Level III cover comes in three shapes, and choosing the wrong one is the usual source of friction later. Retained cover names a Level III of record continuously, sized to your qualification calendar and your procedure churn. Project cover attaches to a defined scope — a contract, a procedure set, a single facility — and ends when that scope does. Interim cover fills a hole that has already opened, and is judged on speed and on what it leaves behind.

Retained cover suits firms whose contracts require a named Level III at all times and whose demand is steady but low. Project cover suits EPCs and fabricators with a defined job and a defined end date. Interim cover suits a firm that has just lost its Level III and now cannot qualify a technician or approve a procedure until somebody is designated. [Interim NDT Level 3 cover](/consulting/interim-ndt-level-3) sets out how that gap is closed, how fast, and what the handover has to contain.

In every shape, the arrangement is documented in the employer's written practice. SNT-TC-1A permits an employer to engage an outside agency Level III for technical work provided the arrangement is written down. NAS 410 goes further: the employer identifies a Responsible Level 3 in writing to act on its behalf in qualification and certification matters, and that person may come from an outside agency. The full role is set out under [ASNT Level III consulting services](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services).

sections.heading: Programme build for a firm that has none
paragraphs: Firms starting an inspection capability from zero — a new NDT contractor, a fabricator bringing examination in-house, an operator building an owner-inspector function — need a programme designed in sequence rather than assembled as problems appear. The sequence is fixed: choose the regime, write the practice, define methods and levels, build the procedure set, establish training and experience records, then qualify the first technician against all of it.

Doing it in that order costs a fraction of retrofitting it. Doing it in reverse — hiring technicians, taking work, then discovering no document supports what was signed — is how firms end up requalifying people who were competent all along, because the evidence trail behind their qualification was never built. Competence and provable competence are different assets, and only one of them survives an audit or a client's supplier qualification questionnaire.

Programme build pairs naturally with getting people through the levels in the first place. [NDT training](/training) covers the classroom and practical hours side, method by method; the programme side covers what those hours must be recorded against for the resulting certificate to mean anything to a customer. Building both together means the first cohort qualifies into a programme that already holds their records correctly, rather than into a filing gap discovered two years later.

sections.heading: Audit and gap assessment against the regime that will actually be applied
paragraphs: A gap assessment is an audit you commission against yourself, run against the regime that will actually be applied to you. That qualifier carries the weight: assessing a programme against SNT-TC-1A when the incoming client contract names CP-189 produces a clean report and a failed audit. CP-189 is an American National Standard written in shall; SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice written in should. CP-189 also carries additional requirements for experience, examinations and record keeping.

The output is a findings list mapped to clause, owner and closure date — not a narrative report that reads well and changes nothing. Findings cluster in four places: written practice currency, procedure control, examination records, and vision test currency. Each has a different fix and a very different lead time. Knowing those lead times before an audit is announced is most of the value, because a missing vision test is a same-week fix and a missing examination paper is a requalification.

[Programme audit and gap assessment](/consulting/ndt-program-audit-gap-assessment) covers the review itself and the closure support that follows it. Closure matters more than the finding: an audit that produces a list nobody works through leaves the programme exactly where it was, except that documentation now exists proving the firm knew. That is a worse position than never having run the assessment, which is why closure support is scoped into the engagement rather than sold separately.

sections.heading: Succession, and the gap that opens when a Level III leaves
paragraphs: When a named Level III leaves, existing certifications remain valid and the approving authority disappears. Until a replacement is designated in the written practice, no new technician can be qualified and no procedure can be approved or revised. Work continues normally until the first procedure change or the first new hire — and then it stops, usually on a week when a client is waiting and nobody has time to run a recruitment process properly.

Succession planning removes that cliff. A named deputy, an overlap period, a transferred record set and a documented handover convert a resignation into an administrative change. The handover pack is the part that gets skipped: examination question banks, procedure revision history, demonstration records and the reasoning behind non-obvious technique decisions all live in one person's head until somebody sits down and writes them out.

Where the departure has already happened, interim cover closes the gap while recruitment runs, and the interim Level III builds the handover pack the permanent appointment will inherit. That sequencing matters more than it looks: an interim engagement that leaves nothing behind recreates the identical cliff eighteen months later, with the same client, the same procedure queue and the same week of lost work.

sections.heading: The method scope constraint that decides who can sign what
paragraphs: Level III certification is granted per method, and authority is bounded by the methods held. A Level III certified in UT and MT can approve UT and MT procedures and grade UT and MT examinations. That signature does not extend to RT or ET, however senior the individual or however long they have worked in the industry. Programmes selling six methods need six methods covered, whether by one person holding all six or several holding a few each.

This is the constraint that quietly invalidates arrangements. A firm engages a Level III, adds a method eighteen months later, and the new method's procedures carry a signature that does not cover them. Every scope statement should list the methods in scope, the regime under which each was certified, and the expiry date. ASNT NDT Level III certifications are renewed on a five-year cycle, either through documented recertification points or by re-examination in each method held.

The regime layer sits above the method layer. SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 are employer-based: your company certifies its own people against your own written practice. ISO 9712 inverts that — an accredited body examines and certifies the individual, and the certificate travels with that person between employers. Many inspectors hold both, SNT-TC-1A for US work and ISO 9712 for international mobility. A programme mixing the two without saying so is the finding an auditor writes first.

sections.heading: How an engagement starts
paragraphs: An engagement starts with a scoping call that establishes four things: the artefact you need at the end, the date somebody is waiting for it, the regime your customer contract names, and the methods in scope. Those four determine everything downstream — delivery model, sequence, and which of your existing records can be reused rather than rebuilt from scratch. Firms consistently underestimate how much of their existing evidence is usable once someone knows what to look for.

Most documentation work runs remotely. Written practice authoring, procedure development, examination banks and gap assessment need your documents and your answers, not a site visit. Site presence is reserved for what genuinely requires it: technique demonstrations on representative geometry, practical examinations, and audit attendance. That split keeps engagements lean regardless of where the facility sits, and keeps the schedule driven by your calendar rather than by travel.

Affordable, accessible, fully customizable — and scoped in writing before anything begins. [Start with a scoping conversation](/contact); demo and quote on request. Bring the contract clause that triggered the enquiry if there is one, because the clause usually names the regime, the methods and the acceptance standard, and settles half the scoping questions before the call has ended.

faq.q: Can an outside consultant certify our NDT technicians?
faq.a: No. Under SNT-TC-1A, certification is an act of the employer and cannot be transferred to an agency. An outside Level III authors the written practice, prepares and grades examinations, approves procedures and provides method oversight — the entire technical chain. Your company signs the certificate, holds the training and experience records, arranges the vision examinations and retains everything for audit. Auditors ask the employer to produce that evidence, never the consultant.

faq.q: Which standard should our written practice be written against?
faq.a: Whichever one your customer contracts name. Aerospace and Nadcap-accredited work invokes NAS 410 or EN 4179. Contracts specifying ANSI/ASNT CP-189 impose a standard written in mandatory language, with additional requirements for experience, examinations and record keeping. Absent an explicit clause, SNT-TC-1A employer-based certification is the default across US industrial work. Declare the choice explicitly in the document and apply it consistently — mixed programmes are the finding auditors write first.

faq.q: How quickly can a written practice or a procedure be turned around?
faq.a: Turnaround is driven by how complete your inputs are, not by the drafting. A procedure written against a code you can name, for a geometry you can describe, with acceptance criteria already fixed by contract, moves fast. A written practice for a firm that has to first decide its regime, its methods and its levels takes a cycle of decisions before drafting starts. Site-dependent work — demonstrations, practical examinations — schedules around access.

faq.q: Do you work outside the United States?
faq.a: Yes. The United States is the primary market, and engagements run across other Western markets on the same basis. Documentation work is regime-specific rather than location-specific: SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 travel with US contracts, NAS 410 and EN 4179 with aerospace supply chains, ISO 9712 where a customer requires third-party certification. Remote delivery covers most of the work; site presence is scheduled where demonstrations, practical examinations or audit attendance require it.

faq.q: What do you need from us to start?
faq.a: The trigger — an audit notice, a contract clause, a resignation, a rejected procedure. Your current written practice if one exists, the methods you perform, the codes your work is governed by, and the customer specification that prompted the enquiry. That is enough to name which of the eight engagements you have and to write a scope. Nothing begins before the deliverable and the date are written down and agreed.

title: Outsourced ASNT NDT Level III: The Role, Signatures and Limits
description: What an outsourced ASNT NDT Level III does day to day, the four signatures an auditor traces, method scope limits, and what your firm must still own itself.
h1: What a Level III of record actually does, month to month
answer: An outsourced Level III holds technical authority inside your programme without joining your payroll. The work is four recurring signatures: the written practice, each NDT procedure, the examination record, and the qualification recommendation, plus method oversight and audit attendance. Certification itself stays with the employer under SNT-TC-1A and cannot be delegated to any agency, however complete the outside work is.
expansion: The role is misread as coverage when it is really custody of a signature chain. SNT-TC-1A requires the employer to prepare a written practice approved by the employer's Level III, and assigns the Level III responsibility for approving and grading qualification examinations. ASME Section V Article 1 T-150 requires written procedures, with a revised procedure prepared and approved by a Level III whenever an essential variable changes. NAS 410 goes further and requires the employer to identify a Responsible Level 3 in writing, a role an outside agency Level 3 can hold. What none of those clauses permits is the outside party issuing the certificate. That stays with the employer, along with training records, documented experience, vision test currency and retained examination papers. An auditor asks the employer for that evidence, and the consultant's name on the procedure does not answer the question.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition) on written practice preparation, Level III approval and grading of examinations, and recommended recertification intervals; ANSI/ASNT CP-189; NAS 410 on the employer-identified Responsible Level 3 and outside agency Level 3 involvement; ASME BPVC Section V Article 1 T-150 on written and revised procedures; ASNT published five-year Level III renewal cycle.

table.note: Five of the six can carry an outside Level III's name. The certificate and the vision record never do — and those two are where most audit findings are actually written.

facets.q: What does an outsourced Level III do in a working month?
facets.a: Reviews and approves procedures against the codes in play, answers technique questions from the field, sets and grades qualification examinations as the calendar requires, updates the written practice when a scheme or contract changes, controls technique demonstrations on representative geometry, and attends audits to defend the programme. Between those events the work is small, which is exactly why the role is outsourced.

facets.q: Which four signatures does an auditor trace?
facets.a: Written practice approval, procedure approval, examination approval and grading, and the qualification recommendation behind each certificate. An auditor follows a technician's certificate backwards through those four and stops at the first gap. Two further records, the certificate itself and the near-vision and colour-contrast examination, never carry an outside name and remain the employer's to produce.

facets.q: How does method scope limit the arrangement?
facets.a: Certification is granted per method, so an outside Level III can only sign inside the methods held. A UT and PT Level III cannot approve an RT procedure or grade an RT examination. Before signing anything, the scope statement must list the methods covered and the regime under which they were certified. Gaps are covered by adding a second Level III, not by stretching one.

facets.q: What are the three ways cover is structured?
facets.a: Retained cover names a Level III of record continuously, sized to your qualification calendar. Project cover attaches to a single scope, contract or procedure set and ends with it. Interim cover fills a gap after a resignation, illness or acquisition and is time-boxed against recruitment, with a handover pack built from day one so the replacement inherits a working programme.

facets.q: What can the arrangement not do?
facets.a: It cannot issue your certificates, hold your records, run your vision examinations, supervise daily field work, or make your programme compliant by signature alone. It also cannot fix a programme whose training hours, documented experience or examination papers were never recorded. Missing history is rebuilt by requalifying people, and no outside signature substitutes for that.

facets.q: What must the firm still own itself?
facets.a: Adoption of the written practice, training and on-the-job experience records, near-vision and colour-contrast examination currency, retained examination papers and scores, the signed certificates, the recertification decision on a maximum five-year cycle under SNT-TC-1A, and records retention. Those six are what an auditor asks the employer to produce, and none of them can be outsourced.

sections.heading: What the role does in a working month
paragraphs: Strip the title away and the role is a queue of small, high-consequence decisions. A procedure arrives for approval because a client changed the acceptance criteria. A technician's qualification comes up because a recertification date landed. A field crew hits a geometry the procedure does not cover and needs a technique variation authorised in writing. A client announces an audit with six weeks' notice. None of these fills a week; every one of them stops work if nobody holds the authority to answer it.

Across a month the recurring items are procedure review and approval against the codes actually in play, technique questions answered in writing, examination setting and grading against the qualification calendar, written practice updates when a scheme edition or a contract changes, control of technique demonstrations on representative geometry, and audit attendance. Where a specific report is challenged rather than the programme, an independent technical review sits alongside — the same discipline applied to output, covered under [NDT report validation](/report-validation).

The rhythm is lumpy rather than light. Qualification cycles, contract wins and audits cluster together, and between clusters demand collapses to almost nothing. That shape — continuously required, intermittently occupied — is the entire economic argument for the arrangement, and it is why the comparison against hiring turns on qualification frequency rather than on how many technicians are on the payroll.

sections.heading: The four signatures an auditor traces
paragraphs: An auditor does not assess your Level III. The auditor picks a technician's certificate and walks backwards through four signatures, stopping at the first one that is missing, unsigned, out of method scope or out of date. Written practice approval. Procedure approval. Examination approval and grading. The qualification recommendation sitting behind the certificate itself. Every other question in the audit is downstream of those four, and most audits never get past them.

SNT-TC-1A anchors the first and the third: the employer prepares a written practice that is on file and approved by the employer's Level III, and the Level III carries responsibility for approving and grading the examinations administered for certification. ASME Section V Article 1 T-150 anchors the second, requiring written procedures and requiring a revised procedure to be prepared and approved by a Level III when an essential variable changes. [Written practice development](/consulting/written-practice-development) covers the document at the top of the chain.

The fourth signature is the one firms get wrong. An outside Level III recommends qualification — attests that training hours, documented experience and examination results satisfy the written practice. The employer then issues the certificate. Those are two separate acts by two separate parties, and putting the consultant's name where the employer's belongs creates a finding rather than closing one. The distinction survives every regime; only the terminology moves.

sections.heading: Method scope: the limit on every signature
paragraphs: Every one of those signatures is bounded by method. Certification is granted method by method, so a Level III certified in UT and PT approves UT and PT procedures and grades UT and PT examinations, and cannot reach RT, ET, MT or VT with the same signature. Seniority does not extend scope. Neither does thirty years of experience, a second regime, or a client's willingness to accept it at the time.

This is where arrangements decay without anyone noticing. A firm engages a Level III covering the four methods it sold at the time. Eighteen months later it wins work in a fifth method, writes a procedure, and files it under a signature that does not cover it. The programme now carries a documented gap that will surface at the next audit, dated precisely to the day that procedure was approved — which is worse than a gap nobody can date.

Two controls prevent it. First, the scope statement lists the methods covered, the regime each was certified under, and the certification expiry: ASNT NDT Level III certifications renew on a five-year cycle, either by documented recertification points or by re-examination. Second, adding a method triggers a scope review before the first procedure is written, not after the first job is sold. Coverage gaps are closed by adding a second Level III, never by stretching one.

sections.heading: Three ways cover is structured
paragraphs: Retained cover names a Level III of record continuously in your written practice. It fits firms whose contracts require a named Level III at all times and whose demand is steady but low — procedure approvals as work changes, examinations on a calendar, a written practice review each year, an audit when a client calls one. What you are buying is availability and continuity of authority rather than a volume of hours.

Project cover attaches to a defined scope and ends with it: a single contract, one facility, a method addition, a procedure set built for one client's specification. It suits EPCs, fabricators and firms taking on work outside their normal envelope for a fixed period. The record it leaves behind is narrower, which is entirely acceptable as long as the written practice states clearly which work the arrangement covered and on what date it ended.

Interim cover fills a hole that already exists — a resignation, a long absence, an acquisition that moved the Level III to another legal entity. It is time-boxed against recruitment and judged by what it leaves behind: a handover pack containing examination banks, procedure revision history, demonstration records and the reasoning behind non-obvious technique calls. [Interim NDT Level 3 cover](/consulting/interim-ndt-level-3) sets out how quickly the gap closes and what closes with it.

sections.heading: What the arrangement cannot do
paragraphs: The arrangement cannot issue your certificates. Under SNT-TC-1A certification is an act of the employer and does not transfer to an agency, however complete the agency's technical work. It cannot hold your records — training hours, documented experience, examination papers and vision test results all live with you and are produced by you at audit. It cannot run your vision examinations; it specifies the requirement, and you arrange, witness and retain the test.

It cannot supervise daily field work. A Level III of record is an approval authority, not a site supervisor, and a programme leaning on the arrangement for day-to-day technical direction has a resourcing problem dressed up as a compliance solution. Nor does a designated Responsible Level 3 by itself close the record-based findings that generate most audit results — vision currency, on-the-job training documentation and retained examination papers stay with the employer regardless.

Most importantly, it cannot retroactively create history. Where training hours were never recorded, experience was never documented, or examination papers were discarded during an office move, no signature reconstructs them. The fix is requalifying people who are almost certainly competent, which costs time, money and morale in that order. That is the argument for putting the arrangement in place before an audit is announced rather than in the six weeks after.

sections.heading: What your firm must still own
paragraphs: Six things stay yours no matter how complete the outside cover is. Adoption of the written practice as your document, not the consultant's. Training and on-the-job experience records for every technician. Near-vision and colour-contrast examination currency. Retained examination papers, scores, dates and invigilation records. The signed certificates themselves. And the recertification decision — SNT-TC-1A recommends a maximum five-year interval across Levels I, II and III — together with records retention behind all of it.

None of those is technically difficult. All of them are administratively fragile, because each depends on somebody maintaining a filing discipline between events that are months apart. The failure pattern is uniform across firm sizes: the technical work is excellent, and the evidence that it happened is scattered across three laptops, a shared drive nobody has mapped, and the inbox of an employee who left last year.

Build the record structure first and the outside arrangement becomes cheap to run. A single register holding, per technician per method, the training hours, experience dates, examination results, vision test date and current certificate revision answers most audit questions from one screen. It also converts the annual written practice review from a week of archaeology into an hour of reading, which is where the arrangement stops feeling like overhead.

sections.heading: How this differs from a project consulting engagement
paragraphs: This role is not the same purchase as a consulting project, and conflating the two causes the most common disappointment in the market. A project engagement is scoped to an artefact and ends: a procedure set delivered, a written practice authored, a programme gap assessment closed out, a fitness-for-service assessment signed. Success is the artefact existing and being defensible. The [full consulting practice catalogue](/consulting) lists those engagements and what each produces.

Level III cover is scoped to an authority and continues. Success is that a signature exists on the day it is needed, in the right method, from a person whose certification is current and whose name appears in your written practice. It is closer to a named-officer arrangement than to a piece of work, and it is evaluated on continuity rather than on deliverables. The wider service description sits under [ASNT Level III consulting services](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services).

The practical difference shows up in how the two are governed. A project is governed by a deliverable and a date. Cover is governed by response time, method scope and continuity — what happens when the named person is unavailable, how a second Level III is named, how quickly a procedure is turned around when a client changes acceptance criteria mid-job. Ask those three questions before signing rather than discovering the answers during a shutdown.

sections.heading: What an auditor asks for, in order
paragraphs: Audits run in a predictable order, and preparing in that order beats preparing exhaustively. The auditor asks for the written practice first, checks its edition against the scheme currently in force, and checks its approval signature against a current Level III certification in the relevant methods. Second, a technician's certificate — chosen by the auditor, not offered by you. Third, the entire evidence chain sitting behind that one certificate.

That chain is training records, documented experience, examination papers and grading, vision test currency, and the qualification recommendation. Fourth comes the procedure covering the job that technician actually performed, and whether the revision in force at the time matches what was done. Fifth, the demonstration record where the referencing code required one. Findings almost never come from the first two steps — they come from steps three and four, where the paper trail thins.

Running that sequence against yourself before an auditor does is the entire content of a gap assessment, and the value sits in the lead times rather than in the findings themselves. A missing vision test is a same-week fix. A missing examination paper is a requalification with a technician off the tools. [Programme audit and gap assessment](/consulting/ndt-program-audit-gap-assessment) covers the review and the closure work that follows it.

sections.heading: When outsourcing stops being the right answer
paragraphs: Outsourcing stops being right when the workload stops being lumpy. A firm running continuous qualification, frequent method additions, multiple concurrent client schemes and permanent audit exposure needs the authority resident rather than scheduled. At that point the arrangement becomes a bottleneck instead of a saving, and the tell is unmistakable: a standing queue of procedures waiting on a signature, and field crews working to drafts.

The comparison is a frequency question, not a headcount question. Count qualification events, procedure revisions and audits per year rather than technicians on the payroll — a forty-person crew in one method generates less Level III demand than a twelve-person crew across five. Published US salary bands are worth reading against that count; [NDT Level 3 salary ranges](/ndt-level-3-salary) sets out what the market pays, because the honest comparison is total annual demand against a full-time cost.

There is a hybrid that works well for firms in between: a resident Level II or quality engineer who owns the records, the calendar and the routine field questions, with an outside Level III holding the signatures and the technical authority. It keeps administration close to the work and authority with certification, which is the split that actually survives an audit. [Describe your situation](/contact) and we will tell you which of the three you are — including when the answer is that you should hire.

faq.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign our written practice?
faq.a: Yes, and it is one of the main reasons firms engage one. SNT-TC-1A requires the written practice to be on file and approved by the employer's Level III, and an outside agency Level III designated in that document satisfies the requirement. An auditor checks two things: that the person holds current certification in the relevant methods, and that the involvement is genuine and documented rather than a name on a cover sheet.

faq.q: Our Level III just resigned — what stops immediately?
faq.a: Existing certifications remain valid, but the approving authority is gone. Until a replacement is designated in the written practice, no new technician can be qualified and no procedure can be approved or revised. Work continues until the first procedure change or the first new hire, then it halts. Interim cover closes the gap while recruitment runs and builds the handover pack the permanent appointment inherits, so the same cliff does not reappear.

faq.q: Which methods can be covered?
faq.a: UT, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET, plus advanced techniques including phased array and TOFD. Certification is granted per method, so every scope statement names the specific methods covered and the regime under which each was certified. Where a programme spans more methods than one Level III holds, the gap is filled by naming a second Level III for those methods rather than by extending an existing signature beyond its scope.

faq.q: Is outsourcing cheaper than hiring a Level III?
faq.a: That turns on qualification frequency, not headcount. Count procedure revisions, qualification events and audits per year. A firm with steady, low demand pays for availability it uses in bursts; a firm with continuous qualification and multiple client schemes needs the authority resident. Published US salary bands for the role give the honest denominator — compare total annual demand against a full-time cost, not one day of either against the other.

faq.q: Does a designated Responsible Level 3 close a Nadcap audit?
faq.a: It satisfies the personnel-authority requirement under NAS 410, which AC7114 assesses, and NAS 410 permits an outside agency Level 3 to hold that designation when the employer identifies them in writing. It does not by itself close the record-based findings that generate most Nadcap results — vision test currency, on-the-job training documentation and retained examination papers stay with the employer and are produced by the employer.

title: NDT Training Denver: NAS 410 Aerospace vs SNT-TC-1A Refinery
description: Denver NDT training splits along two standards: NAS 410 for Lockheed, BAE and Sierra Space, SNT-TC-1A for Suncor Commerce City and the DJ Basin. Choose first.
h1: How Denver's Aerospace-and-Refinery Split Decides Your NDT Certification Route
answer: Denver runs two separate NDT certification systems. Aerospace employers on the Front Range certify to NAS 410, where every requirement is mandatory and Level III examinations are graded by a National Aerospace NDT Board. The Suncor Commerce City refinery and DJ Basin operators certify to SNT-TC-1A, an employer-written practice. Pick the standard before you pick the method or the school.
expansion: The Front Range is one of the few US metros where an NDT candidate can pick the wrong certification and still pass every exam. Colorado holds the nation's second-largest aerospace economy and ranks first per capita for private aerospace employment, per the Colorado Space Coalition — Lockheed Martin alone reports more than 14,000 Colorado employees across a Waterton Canyon campus of over six million square feet. That work certifies under NAS 410, published by the Aerospace Industries Association, where every clause reads "shall" and Level III examinations are graded by a National Aerospace NDT Board rather than by your employer. Ninety miles of the same corridor runs on SNT-TC-1A, a recommended practice your employer rewrites into its own written practice. A Suncor-facing UT Level II and a Lockheed-facing UT Level II are not interchangeable documents, and no volume of classroom hours converts one into the other.
source: ASNT certification requirement and 2026 fee tables (certification.asnt.org); ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A; NAS 410, Aerospace Industries Association; Colorado Space Coalition and Choose Colorado aerospace cluster data; Lockheed Martin Colorado site disclosures; BAE Systems / Ball Aerospace transaction close, 16 February 2024; Sierra Space corporate filings; Suncor Commerce City refinery disclosures and Inspectioneering turnaround reporting, March 2026.
