sections.heading: Trimble County or a Trimble scanner: the Louisville search that means two things
paragraphs: Buyers in this metro search "Trimble 3D scanning Louisville" and mean one of two entirely different things. Some are asking about Trimble instruments — the X7 and X12 scanners and the Trimble Business Center and RealWorks processing chain. Others mean Trimble County Generating Station, the LG&E and KU plant at Bedford roughly forty-five miles upriver, which Louisville-based integrity and engineering crews routinely cover.

Both are legitimate scanning enquiries and they need different answers. On instruments: Trimble hardware is one of several capable platforms alongside Leica and FARO, and the correct choice depends on range, congestion and registration strategy rather than on brand loyalty. On the station: it is a conventional generating-plant capture problem, governed by outage windows and by Kentucky boiler and pressure vessel jurisdiction.

Competing Louisville pages address neither reading, which is why the query sits unanswered. Naming the ambiguity directly is both more useful to the searcher and a straightforward way to serve intent nobody else is serving.

sections.heading: Kentucky boiler and pressure vessel jurisdiction, which no competitor page cites
paragraphs: Pressure equipment in Kentucky is regulated by the Boiler Section of the Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction in Frankfort, under KRS 236.030 and the administrative regulations at 815 KAR 15:025, 15:026 and 15:080. Existing boilers and pressure vessels are inspected in accordance with the National Board Inspection Code, Part 2, as incorporated by reference.

This matters to a scanning scope more than it first appears. Where reality capture supports a repair, an alteration or a re-rating on pressure equipment, the dimensional evidence becomes part of a record an inspector will review, and it has to be traceable — instrument, registration residuals, control points, date, operator. A point cloud delivered without that provenance is a picture, not evidence.

It also sets the boundary of what scanning can and cannot conclude. A scan measures geometry. It does not establish remaining wall thickness, which is an ultrasonic question, and it does not substitute for the inspector's disposition. Being explicit about that boundary is a trust signal to anyone who actually holds the compliance obligation.

sections.heading: Air quality, LDAR and why as-built accuracy has a compliance consequence here
paragraphs: Louisville is unusual in operating its own air regime. The Louisville Metro Air Pollution Control District administers the Strategic Toxic Air Reduction programme, a local rule set with no counterpart in most US metros, and it has driven a substantial reduction in district-wide toxic air emissions since it began.

For a chemical plant in Rubbertown, that regime lands on component counts. Leak detection and repair obligations are defined against populations of valves, flanges, connectors and pumps, and those populations live in exactly the congested pipe racks that are hardest to survey by hand and easiest to capture by scanner.

An accurate as-built model is therefore not only an engineering deliverable. It underpins a defensible component register, and it is one of the few places where reality capture connects directly to a regulatory obligation rather than to a construction schedule.

sections.heading: Where Atlantis differs from the scanning firms ranking above us
paragraphs: The pages currently ranking for Louisville scanning are strong on buildings and heritage — Whiskey Row's cast-iron facades, Old Louisville's Victorian district, Churchill Downs — and essentially silent on process plant. None names Rubbertown, none names a generating station, none cites Kentucky pressure equipment jurisdiction.

Atlantis approaches the same capture as an inspection company. Scans are delivered under ASNT Level III review, tolerances are stated and verified against control rather than asserted, and where the scope touches pressure equipment the deliverable is built to sit in an inspection record. The digital twin layer then carries thickness and inspection history on the geometry instead of in a separate spreadsheet.

For heritage and commercial work, the incumbents are perfectly capable and we say so. For a live chemical plant, a generating station tie-in or a terminal, the requirements are different, and that is the work this page is written for. Request a consultation to scope a site.

facets.q: What does industrial 3D laser scanning in Louisville actually cover?
facets.a: Process piping, reactors, exchangers, tank farms and structural steel in the Rubbertown chemical district; brownfield tie-ins at LG&E's Mill Creek and Cane Run generating stations; terminals and conveyors at Jefferson Riverport; and line-relocation and retrofit capture at the Ford plants, GE Appliance Park and UPS Worldport.

facets.q: Does "Trimble 3D scanning Louisville" mean the scanner or Trimble County?
facets.a: Both, and they are different enquiries. Some searchers mean Trimble instruments such as the X7 and X12 and the Business Center processing chain; others mean Trimble County Generating Station at Bedford, about forty-five miles upriver, which Louisville-based crews cover. Competing pages answer neither.

facets.q: Who regulates pressure equipment in Kentucky?
facets.a: The Boiler Section of the Kentucky Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction in Frankfort, under KRS 236.030 and 815 KAR 15:025, 15:026 and 15:080. Existing boilers and pressure vessels are inspected per the National Board Inspection Code, Part 2, as incorporated by reference.

facets.q: Can a laser scan be used as evidence in a pressure equipment repair record?
facets.a: The dimensional element can, provided its provenance is traceable — instrument, control points, registration residuals, date and operator. A scan measures geometry only; it does not establish remaining wall thickness, which requires ultrasonics, and it does not replace the inspector's disposition.

facets.q: How does scanning support LDAR compliance in Rubbertown?
facets.a: Leak detection and repair obligations under the Louisville Metro APCD STAR programme are defined against populations of valves, flanges, connectors and pumps. Those populations sit in congested pipe racks that are difficult to survey manually, and an accurate as-built model underpins a defensible component register.

facets.q: Can plants be scanned without shutting down?
facets.a: Usually yes, and in this metro it is often the only option — UPS Worldport sorts nightly and the assembly plants cannot stop. Live capture is a planning problem: permit to work, line of sight around moving equipment, and enough station density that congestion does not leave shadow zones in the cloud.

faq.q: What accuracy should a Louisville industrial scan be delivered to?
faq.a: State it as a verified tolerance against control rather than as an instrument specification. Manufacturer accuracy describes the scanner under ideal conditions; what matters on a congested plant is registration residual across the whole network, which should be reported with the deliverable.

faq.q: Which deliverable formats suit downstream piping design?
faq.a: E57 or LAS for the registered cloud, RCP or RCS for Autodesk workflows, and a modelled deliverable in Revit or a plant design application where routing is the objective. The right answer depends on what the receiving engineering team already runs.

title: 3D Laser Scanning Phoenix — Fab, Data Centre and Plant
description: Industrial reality capture across the Phoenix semiconductor corridor, data centre build-out and utility assets, with Part 107 and BTR limits stated.
h1: Industrial 3D Laser Scanning in Phoenix: Semiconductor, Data Centre and Utility Assets
answer: Phoenix is not a refining market and a scanning page that pretends otherwise is not credible here. The metro's reality-capture demand comes from semiconductor fabrication, a gigawatt-scale data centre build-out, aerospace manufacturing, copper processing and utility generation — a different asset mix from the Gulf Coast, needing different capture and different deliverables.
expansion: Arizona has no meaningful crude refining; refined product arrives by pipeline, principally on Kinder Morgan SFPP East Line from El Paso and the West Line from Southern California, both PHMSA-regulated. So the fixed-equipment story here is terminals, tankage and pipeline facilities rather than process units. What replaces it is more demanding. TSMC Fab 21 in north Phoenix and Intel Ocotillo in Chandler mean tool-install as-builts, cleanroom hookup and gas and chemical distribution routing, where a few millimetres of clash decides whether a tool lands on schedule. The data centre corridor from Mesa through Chandler and Goodyear to El Mirage is the fastest-growing capture demand in the metro. Palo Verde Generating Station west of the city, the largest nuclear station in the United States, plus the SRP and APS gas fleet, give a conventional plant scope alongside it.

sections.heading: The licensure boundary, stated plainly
paragraphs: In Arizona, land surveying is a licensed activity regulated by the State Board of Technical Registration. That creates a boundary every honest scanning provider has to state: a registered point cloud and an as-built model are informational deliverables, and they are not a certified boundary survey or a sealed engineering document unless produced under the appropriate registration. It applies equally at TSMC Fab 21 in north Phoenix, at Intel Ocotillo in Chandler and on a Maricopa County site boundary.

Some Phoenix providers disclaim this explicitly. It reads as a weakness only to someone who has not had a project delayed by a deliverable that could not be used for the purpose it was commissioned for. Where a scope genuinely requires certification, the right answer is to say so at proposal stage and bring in a registrant, not to blur the line and discover it at handover.

Atlantis states the boundary the same way. Our deliverables are dimensional and inspection-grade, reviewed by an ASNT Level III where the scope touches pressure equipment, and we are explicit about where a licensed surveyor or a registered engineer has to sign.

sections.heading: Airspace is a real constraint in this metro, not a footnote
paragraphs: Aerial LiDAR and drone photogrammetry are frequently the efficient answer for stockpiles, roof structures, large sites and anything at height. In Phoenix, whether they are available at all depends on where the site sits.

Phoenix Sky Harbor generates Class B airspace over the central metro, and Luke Air Force Base restricted airspace covers a substantial part of the west valley. Both constrain Part 107 operations, and both mean authorisation timelines that have to be built into a programme rather than discovered during mobilisation.

The practical consequence is that a Phoenix capture plan should state, per site, whether aerial capture is available, what authorisation is required, and what the terrestrial fallback is. A proposal that assumes drone access everywhere in this metro has not looked at the map.

sections.heading: Desert conditions change how a scan is planned
paragraphs: Heat and dust are not incidental here. Surface temperatures on exposed steel and concrete through a Phoenix summer affect instrument behaviour and target stability, and airborne dust degrades return quality at range — which is precisely when long-range stations are being used to cover a large site efficiently.

The mitigations are unglamorous and they work: schedule around thermal peaks, shorten station spacing rather than pushing range, use targets rated for the environment, and verify registration residuals on site rather than discovering drift in the office.

Maricopa County Air Quality Department Rule 310 also governs dust control on earthmoving sites, which shapes when ground disturbance and therefore access is happening. Aligning capture with that schedule avoids mobilising into a site that cannot host the work.

sections.heading: What the pages ranking above us do not offer
paragraphs: The current top results split into two groups. One is a national subsurface and utility-locating brand that added laser scanning as a secondary line, where the scanning page is broad and the local content thin. The other is architectural and cultural — Taliesin West, the Orpheum, museums — with industrial appearing as a single word in a vertical list.

Neither addresses the Phoenix asset mix that actually generates recurring capture spend: fab tool installs, data centre shells, utility outages, terminal tankage. Nor does either state the licensure boundary or the airspace constraint, both of which a buyer discovers eventually and would rather know up front.

That is the gap this page is written into. Atlantis brings inspection-grade capture with Level III review, and where the scope is purely architectural we will say that a specialist AEC scanning firm is the better fit. Request a consultation to scope a Phoenix site.

facets.q: Does Phoenix have refineries that need industrial scanning?
facets.a: No. Arizona has no meaningful crude refining capacity, and refined product arrives by pipeline — principally Kinder Morgan's SFPP East Line from El Paso and the West Line from Southern California. The fixed-equipment scope here is terminals, tankage and pipeline facilities rather than process units.

facets.q: What drives most reality-capture demand in Phoenix?
facets.a: Semiconductor fabrication in north Phoenix and Chandler, the data centre corridor from Mesa through Chandler and Goodyear to El Mirage, aerospace manufacturing at Deer Valley and Mesa, utility generation including Palo Verde and the SRP and APS gas fleet, and statewide copper mining and processing.

facets.q: Can a laser scan be used as a certified survey in Arizona?
facets.a: Not by itself. Land surveying is licensed by the Arizona State Board of Technical Registration, so a registered point cloud and an as-built model are informational deliverables unless produced under the appropriate registration. Where a scope needs certification, that should be settled at proposal stage.

facets.q: Is drone LiDAR available across the Phoenix metro?
facets.a: It depends on the site. Class B airspace around Sky Harbor covers the central metro and Luke Air Force Base restricted airspace covers much of the west valley, both constraining Part 107 operations. A capture plan should state per site whether aerial is available, what authorisation is needed and what the terrestrial fallback is.

facets.q: How do desert conditions affect scan accuracy?
facets.a: Heat affects instrument behaviour and target stability on exposed steel and concrete, and airborne dust degrades return quality at range — exactly when long-range stations are being used to cover ground efficiently. Scheduling around thermal peaks and shortening station spacing rather than pushing range are the effective mitigations.

facets.q: What makes semiconductor fab scanning different from plant scanning?
facets.a: Tolerance and access. Tool install as-builts, cleanroom hookup and gas and chemical distribution routing are judged on clash at millimetre scale rather than on visual completeness, and protocol-controlled areas restrict when and how capture can happen. The deliverable has to feed a design model, not a viewer.

faq.q: Do you scan occupied data centres?
faq.a: Yes, and it is common in this metro. The constraints are access control, no interference with live equipment, and working within construction sequencing on phased campuses. Capture is usually repeated across phases rather than done once.

faq.q: Is scanning useful for copper mining assets?
faq.a: Yes — conveyors, crushers, fixed plant and stockpile volumes are all standard scopes. Continuous operation usually means drone or mobile capture rather than static terrestrial stations, with accuracy expectations set accordingly.

title: 3D Laser Scanning Corpus Christi — Refinery Row and LNG
description: Point cloud and as-built capture for Refinery Row, Cheniere LNG at Gregory, Port of Corpus Christi terminals and the Ingleside export corridor.
h1: Industrial 3D Laser Scanning in Corpus Christi: Refinery Row, LNG and the Export Corridor
answer: Corpus Christi is one of the densest industrial capture markets in the United States, and almost none of that shows up on the scanning pages currently ranking for it. Refinery Row, the Cheniere liquefaction trains at Gregory, the Ingleside export terminals and the Port's inner harbour give this metro a scope profile closer to Houston than to a typical mid-size city.
expansion: The refining base alone is substantial: CITGO on the Nueces River, Valero's East and West plants running roughly 370,000 barrels per day combined between light sweet and heavier grades, and Flint Hills Resources East and West at roughly 339,000. Add the Cheniere Corpus Christi Liquefaction facility at Gregory in San Patricio County, where Trains 5 and 6 completed in March and June 2026 alongside the Stage III midscale trains, and the Enbridge Ingleside Energy Center, the largest crude export terminal in the country. Then the industrial diversification most pages miss entirely — Gulf Coast Growth Ventures, the ExxonMobil and SABIC ethane cracker and polyethylene complex at Gregory; Steel Dynamics' flat roll mill at Sinton; the voestalpine hot briquetted iron plant at Portland; and Corpus Christi Army Depot, the largest helicopter maintenance and overhaul facility in the world.
source: Published operator capacity data for CITGO Corpus Christi, Valero Bill Greehey Refineries and Flint Hills Resources Corpus Christi; Cheniere published Corpus Christi Liquefaction and Stage III project status; Port of Corpus Christi Authority published terminal and Ship Channel Improvement Project information; Enbridge Ingleside Energy Center published capacity; TCEQ, Railroad Commission of Texas, PHMSA and US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi jurisdictional scopes; API 653, API 510, API 570 and ASME BPVC Section V.

sections.heading: The LNG trains are the scope most competing pages have not caught up with
paragraphs: Corpus Christi's liquefaction capacity has expanded materially and recently. The Cheniere facility at Gregory now runs eight liquefaction trains with roughly 23 million tonnes per annum of aggregate nominal capacity, with Trains 5 and 6 completing in March and June of 2026, and the Stage III midscale trains adding to that.

Cryogenic service changes what a capture has to deliver. Insulation thickness is substantial and it hides the pipe, so an external scan records the lagging rather than the line — which matters when the model is being used for tie-in design. Where the actual pipe geometry is needed, capture has to be planned around insulation removal or supplemented with other data.

The commissioning and expansion cycle also means a live construction environment adjacent to operating trains, with the access control and permit regime that implies. A capture plan that treats it as an open construction site will not survive contact with the operator.

sections.heading: Export terminals and the marine boundary
paragraphs: Corpus Christi is the largest crude oil export port in the United States by volume, and the Enbridge Ingleside Energy Center is the largest single crude export terminal in the country. That concentrates a specific kind of scanning work: tankage, manifolds, loading arms, dock structure and the transition between shore-side piping and marine transfer equipment.

The regulatory picture at that boundary is layered. Tank inspection sits under API 653; the piping under API 570; the marine transfer operation and the dock structure bring in US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi; and the pipelines feeding the terminals divide between the Railroad Commission of Texas for intrastate and PHMSA for interstate.

A scanning deliverable that is going to support inspection or repair across that boundary needs to be explicit about which asset it covers and to what tolerance, because the receiving parties are different organisations with different acceptance criteria.

sections.heading: Why the pages ranking here are beatable
paragraphs: The current top results are generalist reality-capture and drone shops. The strongest of them names the refineries as geography rather than as assets — it knows Corpus Christi has refineries but not what inspecting or modelling one involves. Another names no scanner brand at all, which is a large credibility gap for an industrial buyer who wants to know whether the instrument suits a congested unit.

The weakest page in the top set names not a single Corpus Christi facility. It ranks on domain factors rather than on relevance, and that is exactly the kind of position a genuinely local, genuinely technical page can take.

Atlantis approaches this as an inspection company that scans, not a scanning company that mentions inspection. Capture is reviewed by an ASNT Level III, tolerances are verified against control, and where the deliverable will sit in an API 510, 570 or 653 record it is built for that from the outset. Request a consultation to scope a Corpus Christi site.

sections.heading: Hurricane season shapes the work calendar
paragraphs: From June through November the Gulf drives a distinct pattern of demand. Pre-storm work concentrates on securing and documenting condition; post-storm work concentrates on rapid external assessment of tankage, floating roofs, seals and structures, where a fast, accurate baseline makes damage assessment quantitative rather than anecdotal.

This is one of the clearest arguments for maintaining a current as-built model rather than commissioning capture reactively. Comparing a post-event scan against a known baseline turns a judgement call about displacement or deformation into a measurement.

Practically, that means scheduling baseline capture outside the season and holding registration control so a repeat survey is genuinely comparable — the same discipline that makes corrosion mapping trendable applies to structural geometry.

facets.q: Which Corpus Christi facilities generate industrial scanning demand?
facets.a: Refinery Row — CITGO, Valero East and West at roughly 370,000 barrels per day combined, and Flint Hills Resources East and West at roughly 339,000; the Cheniere liquefaction trains at Gregory; the Enbridge Ingleside export terminal; Gulf Coast Growth Ventures; Steel Dynamics Sinton; voestalpine at Portland; and Corpus Christi Army Depot.

facets.q: What is different about scanning LNG liquefaction trains?
facets.a: Cryogenic service carries thick insulation, so an external scan records the lagging rather than the pipe itself. Where actual line geometry is needed for tie-in design, capture must be planned around insulation removal or supplemented. Access also sits under a live-operations permit regime rather than open construction rules.

facets.q: Who regulates the assets being scanned in this port?
facets.a: It divides by asset. TCEQ covers air permits and tank programmes, the Railroad Commission of Texas covers intrastate pipelines, PHMSA covers interstate pipelines and LNG facility integrity, and US Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi covers marine transfer and dock structure. A deliverable crossing that boundary should say which asset it addresses.

facets.q: How does turnaround season affect scheduling?
facets.a: It concentrates demand. Spring and autumn turnaround windows on Refinery Row set the calendar for most unit capture in this metro, which means mobilisation slots are contested and planning has to start well before the window rather than when the scope is finalised.

facets.q: Is scanning useful after a hurricane?
facets.a: Yes, and it is far more useful when a baseline already exists. Comparing a post-event scan against a known, registration-controlled baseline turns questions about displacement, settlement or roof and seal deformation into measurements rather than judgement calls. Baseline capture is best scheduled outside the June to November season.

facets.q: Does the Army Depot work differ from refinery work?
facets.a: Yes. Corpus Christi Army Depot is a controlled-access facility and the largest helicopter maintenance and overhaul operation in the world, so imagery restrictions and access protocol dominate planning. The capture itself is facility, hangar structure and tooling as-built rather than process plant.

faq.q: Can you capture a unit while it is running?
faq.a: Often yes, subject to permit to work and to line of sight around live equipment. Congested pipe racks need denser station spacing to avoid shadow zones, and the capture plan should state how coverage will be verified rather than assumed.

faq.q: What deliverable does a tank inspection scope need?
faq.a: For API 653 work the useful outputs are shell verticality and out-of-roundness, roof and floor geometry and settlement survey data referenced to a repeatable datum. The scan supports the geometric elements; remaining thickness still comes from ultrasonics.

title: 3D Laser Scanning San Francisco Bay — Refinery and MOTEMS
description: Reality capture for Bay Area refineries, renewable conversions and marine oil terminals, built around MOTEMS audits and Cal/OSHA refinery PSM.
h1: Industrial 3D Laser Scanning in the San Francisco Bay Area: Refineries, Conversions and Marine Terminals
answer: Bay Area industrial scanning is concentrated in the northern refining corridor rather than in San Francisco itself. Chevron Richmond, PBF Martinez, Valero Benicia and the Phillips 66 Rodeo and Martinez renewable conversions sit within a short radius, and each is generating existing-conditions capture work for a different reason.
expansion: The conversions are the live opportunity. Phillips 66 has ended petroleum refining at Rodeo and now runs renewable fuels there, and the former Marathon Martinez refinery operates as Martinez Renewable Fuels — both projects where accurate existing-conditions capture is a precondition for retrofit design rather than a nice-to-have. Valero has given notice to end refining operations at Benicia by the end of April 2026, which puts decommissioning planning, demolition sequencing and as-built documentation on a dated timeline that no competing scanning page in this market mentions. Alongside them sits a regulatory driver unique to California: MOTEMS, the Marine Oil Terminal Engineering and Maintenance Standards in Title 24 Part 2 Chapter 31F of the California Building Code, which requires periodic above- and below-waterline audits of marine oil terminals to demonstrate continued fitness for purpose.

sections.heading: MOTEMS is the strongest Bay Area hook, and no competitor page uses it
paragraphs: Marine oil terminals in California are governed by MOTEMS, administered by the State Lands Commission Marine Environmental Protection Division under Title 24 Part 2 Chapter 31F of the California Building Code. Terminals must undergo periodic audits above and below the waterline covering structural, seismic, geotechnical, mooring, berthing, fire protection, piping, mechanical, electrical and corrosion evaluation, and demonstrate continued fitness for purpose.

Reality capture supports several of those elements directly. Structural geometry, mooring and berthing configuration, and the deformation history of a wharf are all dimensional questions, and a registration-controlled scan gives an auditor a comparable measurement rather than a description.

Terminals submit Executive Summary Tables to the Commission annually by the end of January, which puts a recurring, dated demand into the calendar. A scanning provider who understands that cycle is offering something categorically different from one selling generic as-built services, and not one page in the current top five for Bay Area scanning references MOTEMS at all.

sections.heading: California refinery PSM is stricter than the federal standard
paragraphs: Cal/OSHA operates a refinery-specific process safety management standard at Title 8 CCR section 5189.1, on top of general PSM at 5189. It carries requirements the federal standard does not, including damage mechanism review and an explicit hierarchy of hazard controls.

Damage mechanism review is where accurate as-built information earns its place. Identifying credible mechanisms for a circuit depends on knowing what the circuit actually is — its routing, its dead legs, its injection points, its supports — and on many older Bay Area units the drawings and the plant diverged decades ago.

Contra Costa County adds its Industrial Safety Ordinance on top, applying county-level process safety requirements to the Richmond and Martinez refineries. The practical effect is that documentation quality is scrutinised more heavily here than in most US refining regions, which raises the value of a defensible dimensional record.

sections.heading: Decommissioning is a scanning scope people forget to plan for
paragraphs: With Valero having given notice to end refining at Benicia by the end of April 2026, the Bay Area has a live decommissioning case. Decommissioning generates capture demand that differs from operational work: the objective is a complete record of what exists before it is removed, together with geometry accurate enough to plan demolition sequencing and lifts.

It is also the point at which an operator discovers what its drawings are worth. Retiring an asset requires knowing where everything is, including buried and encased services that never made it onto a revision, and a scan captures what is visible while flagging what is not.

The same applies in reverse to the conversions at Rodeo and Martinez, where retrofit design has to start from actual existing conditions rather than from a design basis that is decades old. Both directions are existing-conditions problems, and both are poorly served by scanning pages written for commercial real estate.

sections.heading: What the incumbent pages actually are
paragraphs: The pages ranking above us here share one characteristic: they are templates. One is a national subsurface and utility brand whose industrial credibility lives on national service pages and is never bound to the Bay Area. Another runs to several thousand words and yet names no San Francisco neighbourhood, building, agency or ordinance. A third is a Boston company running an interchangeable cities template with San Francisco as one slot among many.

None of them mentions MOTEMS, Cal/OSHA 5189.1, the Contra Costa Industrial Safety Ordinance, BAAQMD, or a single named refinery in the corridor. That is not a small gap for a buyer whose actual problem is a terminal audit or a conversion retrofit.

Atlantis is an inspection organisation first, with capture reviewed by an ASNT Level III and deliverables built to sit in an inspection or audit record. For commercial interiors and heritage work in the city itself, a specialist AEC scanning firm may well be the better fit, and we will say so. Request a consultation to scope a Bay Area site.

facets.q: Where is Bay Area industrial scanning demand actually concentrated?
facets.a: In the northern refining corridor rather than in San Francisco proper — Chevron Richmond, PBF Martinez, Valero Benicia, and the Phillips 66 Rodeo and Martinez renewable conversions, all within a short radius in Contra Costa and Solano counties, together with the marine oil terminals serving them.

facets.q: What is MOTEMS and how does scanning support it?
facets.a: The Marine Oil Terminal Engineering and Maintenance Standards, in Title 24 Part 2 Chapter 31F of the California Building Code and administered by the State Lands Commission. Terminals undergo periodic above- and below-waterline audits covering structural, seismic, mooring, piping and corrosion evaluation, and registration-controlled capture supplies comparable dimensional evidence.

facets.q: How does California refinery PSM differ from the federal standard?
facets.a: Cal/OSHA operates a refinery-specific standard at Title 8 CCR section 5189.1 in addition to general PSM at 5189, carrying requirements the federal rule does not — notably damage mechanism review and an explicit hierarchy of hazard controls. Contra Costa County adds its Industrial Safety Ordinance on top for Richmond and Martinez.

facets.q: Why do refinery conversions need existing-conditions capture?
facets.a: Because retrofit design has to start from what is actually there. The Rodeo and Martinez sites converted from petroleum to renewable fuels, and on units of that age the drawings and the plant diverged long ago. Accurate capture is a precondition for routing and tie-in design rather than an optional deliverable.

facets.q: What does decommissioning capture need to deliver?
facets.a: A complete record of what exists before removal, with geometry accurate enough to plan demolition sequencing and lifts. It is also where drawing quality gets tested, since retiring an asset requires knowing where everything is — including services that never made it onto a revision. Valero's Benicia notice puts this on a dated timeline.

facets.q: Do you handle commercial and heritage scanning in San Francisco itself?
facets.a: The city contributes commercial, seismic retrofit and heritage work, and specialist AEC scanning firms are strong at it. Our advantage is inspection-grade capture on process plant, tankage and marine structures, so for a purely architectural interior scope we will say when another provider is the better fit.

faq.q: Can below-waterline structure be captured?
faq.a: Not by terrestrial laser scanning, which is a line-of-sight method above water. Below-waterline audit elements under MOTEMS use diver or ROV survey and sonar methods; the scan covers the above-water structure and ties the two records to a common datum.

faq.q: How current does an as-built need to be for damage mechanism review?
faq.a: Current enough that the circuit in the model matches the circuit in the plant, including dead legs, injection points and supports. Where a unit has been revamped since the last documentation update, the review is being performed against a plant that no longer exists.

title: ASME Section V Article 9: Visual Examination Rules
description: ASME Section V Article 9 visual examination: 100 fc (1,000 lux) at the surface, eye within 24 in. at 30 degrees or more, remote resolution equal to direct.
h1: ASME V Article 9 — What Visual Examination Actually Requires
answer: ASME Section V Article 9 governs visual examination technique, not acceptance. It requires a written procedure addressing the Table T-921 variables, direct viewing with the eye within 24 in. (600 mm) of the surface at 30 degrees or more, a minimum of 100 fc (1,000 lux) on the surface, and remote systems proven equivalent to direct sight. Acceptance criteria come from the referencing code.
expansion: Article 9 is a technique document. It tells you how to look: the written procedure and the variables in Table T-921, direct examination with the eye within 24 in. (600 mm) of the surface at 30 degrees or more, at least 100 fc (1,000 lux) of light on the surface, remote systems with resolution at least equivalent to direct sight, and translucent examination as a supplement using a light source behind the part. It does not tell you what is acceptable. Every threshold comes from the referencing code: ASME VIII Division 1 for vessel weld finish, ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 Table 8.1 for structural welds, Section XI for in-service categories. Most Article 9 findings are not missed indications. They are missing evidence: no light reading taken at the point of examination, no procedure demonstration on file, no resolution check for the borescope that replaced the eye.
source: ASME BPVC Section V, Article 9 (Visual Examination), including T-910 Scope, T-921 Written Procedure Requirements and Table T-921, T-950 Techniques (T-951 direct, T-952 remote, T-953 translucent), T-980 Evaluation and T-990 Documentation; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 1 (General Requirements), T-120 and T-150; ASME BPVC Section VIII Division 1, UW-35 and UW-36; ASME BPVC Section IX, QW-194; ASME BPVC Section XI, IWA-2210 (VT-1, VT-2, VT-3); ASME B31.3 Process Piping, para. 344.2 and Table 341.3.2; AWS D1.1/D1.1M Structural Welding Code — Steel, Clause 8 and Table 8.1; ASNT SNT-TC-1A and ANSI/ASNT CP-189.

facets.q: Does ASME Section V Article 9 contain acceptance criteria?
facets.a: No. Article 9 is a technique article. Its evaluation clause directs you to the acceptance standards of the referencing code section, which is where every threshold lives: ASME VIII Division 1 for vessel weld finish and fillet weld profile, ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 Table 8.1 for structural steel, API 650 and API 653 for tanks. A report citing only Article 9 for acceptance is incomplete and will draw a finding.

facets.q: How close must the eye be for direct visual examination?
facets.a: Direct visual examination is normally performed with the eye within 24 in. (600 mm) of the surface and at an angle of not less than 30 degrees to that surface. Both figures are limits rather than working targets. Mirrors may be used to improve the angle of vision and magnifiers may be used to assist, but the geometry stated in the procedure must be the geometry that the procedure demonstration actually covered.

facets.q: Is the 100 foot-candle requirement measured at the lamp or the surface?
facets.a: At the surface being examined. A minimum of 100 fc (1,000 lux) must reach the examination surface, not the light source, not the walkway and not the QA bench. Article 9 also requires that the light source, the technique and the light level verification are demonstrated once, documented and kept on file. Auditors ask for a calibrated meter, the reading taken at the point of examination, and evidence the same lamp and stand-off were used.

facets.q: Can a borescope, crawler or drone camera satisfy Article 9?
facets.a: Yes, under the remote visual technique, provided the system has resolution capability at least equivalent to direct visual observation. That is a performance requirement to be demonstrated with the deployed equipment at the real working distance, real light level and real display, with any video compression in the path. A resolution target photographed in the field and filed with the report settles the question years later far better than an equipment datasheet.

facets.q: Are VT-1, VT-2 and VT-3 defined in ASME Section V Article 9?
facets.a: No. VT-1, VT-2 and VT-3 are in-service examination categories defined by ASME Section XI, IWA-2210, for nuclear components: VT-1 for surface discontinuities and conditions, VT-2 for leakage detection, VT-3 for general mechanical and structural condition including clearances, loose parts and debris. Section XI imposes its own resolution demonstration. Writing VT-2 per ASME V Article 9 on a report conflates two codes and is an immediate finding.

facets.q: What must an Article 9 visual examination report contain?
facets.a: Enough to reconstruct the examination without the examiner present: the procedure number and revision, the technique used, the examiner and certification level, the date, the lighting used and its verification, the surface condition and any preparation, the extent and location of coverage, the referencing code acceptance paragraph, the results, and the disposition of any indication. Reports that record only accepted or rejected cannot be defended once the surface has been coated.

sections.heading: What Article 9 Covers, and What It Deliberately Does Not
paragraphs: Article 9 of ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section V is the method article for visual examination. Its scope covers the act of looking at a surface and recording what was seen: the written procedure, the personnel and equipment, the three recognised techniques of direct, remote and translucent examination, the evaluation step and the documentation that has to outlive the job. It is one of the shortest articles in Section V and one of the most frequently misapplied, because readers arrive expecting acceptance criteria and Article 9 does not carry any.

What it excludes matters as much as what it contains. Article 9 does not define acceptable weld reinforcement, undercut, arc strikes or surface porosity. It does not define the in-service examination categories VT-1, VT-2 and VT-3, which belong to Section XI. It does not cover leak testing, which is Article 10. It does not itself certify personnel; qualification flows from Article 1 and the employer written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, ANSI/ASNT CP-189 or ISO 9712 as the referencing code permits.

The practical consequence for a QA manager is that an Article 9 procedure is incomplete standing alone. It must name the referencing code and the acceptance paragraph it serves, and it must be reviewed when that reference changes edition. Where the procedure set needs to be technically owned rather than copied from a template, that authority is the substance of [ASNT Level III consulting](/consulting).

sections.heading: Direct Visual: the 24-Inch and 30-Degree Rule People Misread
paragraphs: Direct visual examination under Article 9 is normally performed where access permits the eye to be placed within 24 in. (600 mm) of the surface being examined, at an angle of not less than 30 degrees to that surface. Mirrors are expressly permitted to improve the angle of vision, and magnifying aids are permitted to assist. Both numbers are outer limits. An undercut call made at 24 in. and exactly 30 degrees is a marginal call, and marginal calls are the ones that come back.

The recurring misreading is the angle datum. Thirty degrees is measured from the surface, not from the normal to the surface. At 30 degrees from the surface the examiner is looking along the weld toe at a shallow rake; at 30 degrees from the normal the view is nearly face-on, which is a far more generous geometry than the code allows. An auditor who redraws the angle on a procedure sketch and finds it dimensioned from the normal has a documented finding without ever visiting site.

The second misreading is trading distance against magnification. Article 9 permits aids; it does not permit substituting a 10x loupe at 40 in. for the stated geometry unless the procedure demonstration actually supports that arrangement. Record the geometry and the demonstration together. Examiners trained against the real geometry rather than a slide deck stop generating this finding, which is the practical point of structured [NDT training and certification](/training).

sections.heading: Illumination: 100 fc Is a Floor, Measured at the Surface
paragraphs: Article 9 sets a minimum light intensity of 100 fc (1,000 lux) on the surface to be examined, and requires that the light source, the technique used and the light level verification be demonstrated one time, documented and maintained on file. That last requirement is where the audit trail begins and where most programmes are thinnest, because the demonstration is usually done once by someone who has since left and never repeated when the lamp was replaced.

The reading is taken at the examination surface, not at the lamp. A 500 W floodlight at three metres in an open yard at dusk will not put 100 fc into the root of a nozzle-to-shell weld inside a vessel, and a meter held at chest height in the walkway proves nothing about the surface. Auditors ask for three items in sequence: the light meter calibration certificate in date, the reading taken at the point and orientation of examination, and evidence that the same lamp and stand-off distance were used in the recorded demonstration.

Where the referencing code demands more than 100 fc, more applies, and some in-service applications substitute a resolution check for a bare lux figure. Free-text light readings on paper field sheets are the ones that go missing. Capturing the reading against the weld number and the report inside [inspection management software](/erp) means the value is still attached to the examination three years later when a client or a regulator asks how the surface was lit.

sections.heading: Remote Visual: Proving Equivalence to the Naked Eye
paragraphs: The remote visual technique permits aids in place of direct observation — mirrors, telescopes, borescopes, fibrescopes, cameras and other suitable instruments — provided the system has resolution capability at least equivalent to that obtainable by direct visual observation. That single sentence carries the entire crawler, drone and video-probe industry. It is a performance requirement, not a permission slip, and equivalence has to be shown rather than asserted.

Equivalence must be demonstrated with the actual system as deployed: the same working distance, the same lighting, the same lens, the same display, and any video compression sitting in the signal path. A camera that resolves a fine line at 300 mm on a bench under laboratory lighting does not automatically resolve it at six metres inside a dark column through a wide-angle lens with a lossy encoder between the sensor and the screen. Frame rate, monitor size and gamma are all part of the examination system and all belong in the procedure.

The practical discipline is simple. Build a resolution target, photograph it in the field with the deployed system at the extremes of the procedure, and file that image with the report. When a remote examination is challenged two years later, the field image ends the argument. Where remote data is the only surviving record of a surface that has since been coated, lined or buried, [independent review of the inspection reports](/report-validation) is worth considerably more than a re-examination that is no longer physically possible.

sections.heading: Translucent Visual Examination and Where It Still Applies
paragraphs: Translucent visual examination is a supplement to direct visual examination, using an artificial light source placed behind the object so that light passes through the material and reveals internal discontinuities as variations in transmitted intensity. The direct visual requirements still apply on the viewing side, and the light source must be of sufficient intensity to illuminate and diffuse the light evenly across the area of interest without glare that masks the very variations being sought.

In pressure equipment it is uncommon, but it appears in glass-reinforced plastic tankage, translucent linings and laminate lay-up work where dry patches, voids, delaminations and inclusions show clearly against transmitted light. Where it appears in a procedure copied from a template and no translucent material exists anywhere on the contract, remove it. An auditor reading a procedure that claims a technique will ask to see that technique demonstrated, and an undemonstrated technique in a live procedure is a finding created entirely by cut and paste.

sections.heading: Where the Acceptance Criteria Actually Live
paragraphs: The evaluation clause of Article 9 hands acceptance back to the referencing code section, and the referencing code is where the arguments happen. For unfired pressure vessels, ASME Section VIII Division 1 governs weld finish and reinforcement limits and fillet weld profile. For process piping, ASME B31.3 sets visual examination in para. 344.2 with acceptance in Table 341.3.2, graded by fluid service. For structural steel, AWS D1.1 Clause 8 and Table 8.1 apply, with different criteria for statically and cyclically loaded members. For welder performance test coupons, ASME Section IX carries its own visual requirements at QW-194.

Two consequences follow. First, the same weld can pass under one referencing code and fail under another, so the report must name the acceptance paragraph, not merely the method. Second, a contract that invokes a client specification more restrictive than the code has silently changed the acceptance criteria, and the procedure must reflect that. The most expensive Article 9 disputes are not about whether an indication existed but about which document the parties were measuring it against.

Site teams should keep the acceptance reference on the report line itself rather than in a header note that gets truncated when the record is exported. Where multiple codes run on one project, a single controlled matrix of weld category against acceptance paragraph, maintained by the Level III and reissued when the specification changes, prevents the mixed-code reporting that generates rework at handover.

sections.heading: VT-1, VT-2 and VT-3 Belong to Section XI, Not Article 9
paragraphs: ASME Section XI, IWA-2210, defines the in-service visual examination categories used on nuclear components. VT-1 is directed at detecting discontinuities and imperfections on component surfaces, including cracking, wear, corrosion and erosion. VT-2 is directed at detecting evidence of leakage from pressure-retaining components. VT-3 addresses general mechanical and structural condition — clearances, settings, physical displacements, loose or missing parts, debris, corrosion and wear. Each carries its own resolution demonstration requirements, which are not the Article 9 requirements.

Reports that read VT-2 examination performed in accordance with ASME Section V Article 9 conflate two codes and are corrected on sight by any experienced nuclear auditor. The correct construction names Section XI for the category and its resolution demonstration, and Section V Article 9 only where Section XI invokes it. Getting this wrong in a written practice propagates into every certificate issued under it, which is why the mapping between category, technique and demonstration should be settled once at the procedure level rather than argued weld by weld.

sections.heading: The Written Procedure, Table T-921 and Procedure Demonstration
paragraphs: Article 9 requires a written procedure and Table T-921 lists the requirements it must address, identifying which are essential variables and which are nonessential. Typical entries include the technique used, the surface condition and method of preparation, the method of examination, whether direct or remote, the lighting and viewing aids, the sequence of examination, the data to be tabulated and any post-examination cleaning. A change in an essential variable requires the procedure to be requalified and revised; a change in a nonessential variable requires revision only.

The procedure must also be demonstrated to be adequate, and the demonstration record is the document most often missing. The demonstration should be run at the least favourable conditions the procedure permits — the maximum viewing distance and the minimum illumination — and should establish that a fine detail on the order of 1/32 in. (0.8 mm) can be resolved on the surface in question. Demonstrating on a clean bench under bright light and then working at arm's length in a dark vessel is exactly the mismatch auditors probe.

Keep the demonstration record physically attached to the procedure revision it supports. When the procedure is revised for a new referencing code or a different remote camera, the old demonstration no longer covers it. Programmes that treat the demonstration as a one-off exercise from the year the procedure was first written accumulate a quiet and growing gap between what is written and what is done.

sections.heading: Documentation, Records and the Findings That Recur
paragraphs: Article 9 requires a written report and the records that support it, and the referencing code frequently adds a checklist or a specific report format. A defensible visual examination record identifies the procedure and revision, the technique, the examiner and certification level, the date, the lighting used and its verification, the surface condition and preparation, the extent and location of coverage, the referencing code acceptance paragraph, the results and the disposition of every indication. A report that says only accepted cannot be defended once the surface is painted.

The findings that recur are consistent across industries. Light readings recorded at the lamp rather than the surface. Light meters out of calibration. The 30-degree angle dimensioned from the normal. No procedure demonstration record, or a demonstration run under conditions more favourable than the procedure permits. Remote camera systems with no resolution equivalence evidence. Near-vision examinations expired, which is a written practice requirement rather than an Article 9 one but voids the examination all the same. Acceptance criteria cited as Article 9 instead of the referencing code.

None of these are examination failures. They are record failures, and they are cheap to prevent and expensive to remediate after the fact, because remediation usually means re-examining a surface that is now insulated, coated or in service. A gap review of the procedure set, the demonstration records and a sample of completed reports, run before the client audit rather than after it, is the least costly point at which any of this can be fixed. If that review is useful to you, [start with a consultation](/contact).

faq.q: Does Article 9 require a certified Level II visual examiner?
faq.a: Article 9 does not itself set the certification level. Personnel qualification flows from Section V Article 1 and the referencing code section, which normally requires certification under the employer written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, ANSI/ASNT CP-189 or ISO 9712. Many referencing codes and client specifications require Level II for interpretation and Level III approval of the procedure. Check the contract, then make the written practice match it, rather than assuming a default.

faq.q: How often must the light meter be calibrated and readings taken?
faq.a: Article 9 requires the light source, technique and light level verification to be demonstrated once, documented and kept on file. Calibration interval and the frequency of field readings come from your quality system and the client specification, and annual meter calibration with a reading recorded at each examination location is the practice that survives audit. Programmes that record light levels only at the demonstration and never again are the ones that struggle to defend a challenged examination.

faq.q: Does Article 9 apply to in-service inspection or only new construction?
faq.a: It applies wherever the referencing code invokes it. Section V is a methods manual; the referencing code decides when Article 9 is used. It is commonly invoked for new construction under Section VIII and B31.3, and also for in-service examinations where the owner-user specification calls for it. In nuclear in-service work under Section XI, the examination categories and their resolution demonstrations govern, and Article 9 applies only where Section XI invokes it.

faq.q: What is the difference between Article 9 and AWS D1.1 visual inspection?
faq.a: They answer different questions. Article 9 describes how the examination is performed and documented. AWS D1.1 Clause 8 and Table 8.1 give the acceptance criteria for structural welds, with separate limits for statically and cyclically loaded connections. On a structural contract the acceptance criteria are D1.1, and the technique controls may be D1.1 or Article 9 depending on the specification. Mixing the two on one report is a common source of disputed rejections.

faq.q: Can magnifiers and mirrors be used under Article 9?
faq.a: Yes. Mirrors may be used to improve the angle of vision and magnifiers or other aids may be used to assist the examination. The condition is that the aids are named in the written procedure and covered by the procedure demonstration. An examiner who introduces a borescope or a magnifier that the procedure never mentioned has stepped outside the qualified technique, which is a finding independent of whether the call itself was correct.

title: ASME Section V Article 7: MT Technique and Field Checks
description: ASME Section V Article 7 magnetic particle examination: 10 lb AC and 40 lb DC yoke lift checks, two fields 90 degrees apart, 3 gauss residual limit.
h1: Magnetic Particle Examination to ASME Section V Article 7
answer: ASME Section V Article 7 is the method standard for magnetic particle examination of ferromagnetic material. It fixes the technique options, requires two magnetisations about 90 degrees apart, sets field adequacy verification by lifting force or tangential gauge, and limits residual field after demagnetisation. It contains no accept or reject criteria: the referencing code section supplies those.
expansion: Article 7 sits inside ASME Section V as a method article. It tells you how to magnetise, how to apply particles, how to light the surface and how to prove the field was adequate, and it stops there. Nothing in Article 7 tells you whether an indication is acceptable. That decision belongs to the referencing code section, whether that is Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 6, Section I, B31.3 or a client specification, and confusing the two is the most common structural error in an MT procedure. The requirements that actually bite in the field are the two-direction rule, field adequacy verification at defined points in the job rather than once a year, wet bath concentration inside the centrifuge band, UV-A intensity measured at the surface being examined, and a residual field check after demagnetisation. Each of those is an objective measurement that leaves a record, which is exactly why an auditor samples them first.
source: Sources: ASME BPVC Section V, Article 7 (Magnetic Particle Examination) and Article 1 (General Requirements); SE-709 / ASTM E709; SE-1444 / ASTM E1444; ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 6; ISO 9934-1 and ISO 9934-2.
